passage:
Class 4 notes, Tanuja, class teacher
During morning assembly, Zeenat tripped on the step while carrying the attendance register to the stage. She didn't fall, only wobbled, and caught herself on the rail. Back in class she sat with her head down on her arms. At lunch she told me, "Everyone saw. They'll call me Wobbly till Class 10."
I asked her to look around. Bilal was hunting for his lost eraser, Gauri was worried about her spelling test, and two girls were arguing over whose turn it was on the swing. Nobody had mentioned the step.
Tomorrow I'll ask Zeenat to carry the register again, and I'll quietly tell her how I once dropped a whole box of chalk in front of the principal.

qa.q: What was Zeenat carrying when she tripped?
qa.a: She was carrying the attendance register to the stage.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Zeenat that everyone will call her Wobbly till Class 10?
qa.a: Zeenat feels so embarrassed that the wobble seems huge from the inside, and she imagines every eye was on her, even though the others were busy with erasers, spelling and the swing. 😰

qa.q: Why is Tanuja's plan to let Zeenat carry the register again a good choice?
qa.a: Doing it again soon lets Zeenat see that nobody remembers, which shrinks the fear before it grows.

qa.q: What was that assembly like for Gauri, who was worried about her spelling test?
qa.a: Gauri was probably so busy with her own worry that she never noticed the wobble at all.

grounding: A teacher notes a girl who wobbled at assembly sure everyone will remember, while classmates were busy with their own worries.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today in science Miss asked what plants breathe in, and I said OXYGEN, really loud. Wrong! It's carbon dioxide. I wanted to crawl under the bench. I was SURE everyone was laughing inside.
At break I told Keerthana, "The whole class will remember this forever."
She blinked. "When did you say that?"
She didn't even remember! She was busy thinking about her dance practice. Then Rehan asked me for a spare pencil like nothing had happened.
Maybe people don't keep a list of my mistakes. Maybe they keep lists of their own.
Still, I'm going to read the plant chapter twice. 😅
Ayesha

qa.q: What answer did Ayesha give in science?
qa.a: Ayesha said OXYGEN, really loud.

qa.q: Why was Ayesha so sure everyone was laughing inside?
qa.a: Ayesha felt so embarrassed that the mistake seemed enormous, and it felt obvious that the whole class had noticed and would keep it in mind.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha change her mind, and what could Ayesha try the next time a mistake feels huge?
qa.a: Asking Keerthana showed that nobody remembered; next time Ayesha could check with a friend before deciding everyone is laughing. 🙂

qa.q: What was that science lesson like for Keerthana?
qa.a: Keerthana was busy thinking about dance practice, so the wrong answer barely registered for her.

grounding: A child who gives a wrong answer is sure the class will remember, then finds Keerthana didn't even notice.

passage:
At the gurdwara sports day in their village near Moga, Jasleen tripped in the sack race and rolled right onto the chalk line. She got up with dust on her salwar and finished last. For the rest of the afternoon she stood behind a tent pole, sure the whole village was pointing at her.
"Everyone saw me fall," she whispered to Rajni.
Rajni was licking jalebi syrup off her fingers. "Fall when?"
Across the ground, the boys were arguing about the tug-of-war rope, the aunties were counting prize cups, and the sack-race winner was crying because his sack had torn.
Jasleen came out from behind the pole, just a little.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen stand for the rest of the afternoon?
qa.a: She stood behind a tent pole.

qa.q: Why does Jasleen believe the whole village was pointing at her?
qa.a: The fall felt so big to her that she assumed it was the biggest thing everyone else had seen too.

qa.q: What turning point brought Jasleen out from behind the pole?
qa.a: Rajni's "Fall when?" showed that even her friend hadn't noticed, and she could see everyone busy with their own things. 🙂

qa.q: How was the sack race for the winner, compared with how Jasleen saw it?
qa.a: The winner was busy crying over a torn sack, far too caught up to think about Jasleen's fall.

grounding: A village girl who fell in a race is sure everyone saw, while others were busy with their own troubles.

passage:
Dalia, nine, had one line in the school play in Amman: "The river is rising!" When the moment came, she said, "The rising is river!"
A few children giggled. Dalia's face burned all the way through the final song. At home she refused dinner. "Everyone heard. Everyone will remember forever. I'm never going back."
Her brother Siddiq, who had been in the same play as a tree, looked up from his plate. "What did you say wrong?"
"You were right there!"
"I was trying not to sneeze," Siddiq said. "My leaves were itchy."
The next morning at the school gate, Dalia's best friend ran up. "Did you see my crown fell off? I was so embarrassed!"
Dalia hadn't seen that at all.

qa.q: What did Dalia say instead of 'The river is rising!'?
qa.a: She said, "The rising is river!"

qa.q: How did Dalia feel after her mistake, and what shows it?
qa.a: Dalia felt deeply embarrassed; her face burned through the final song, she refused dinner and said everyone would remember forever.

qa.q: What could Dalia notice from Siddiq and her friend next time she makes a slip?
qa.a: She could remember that Siddiq didn't notice because of his itchy leaves and her friend was busy worrying about her crown, so most people are thinking about their own worries.

qa.q: How might Dalia's best friend have felt about the crown falling off?
qa.a: Her best friend felt embarrassed, just like Dalia, and probably thought everyone had seen the crown, even though Dalia hadn't noticed at all.

grounding: It shows a girl who fumbled her line believing everyone saw, while others were busy with their own worries.

passage:
At the swimming club in Chandigarh, the Saturday class lined up at the pool edge. Amandeep, ten, walked forward and slipped on the wet tiles, landing on his bottom with a loud slap. His face went red. He was sure the whole class had turned to look.
For the rest of the lesson he stayed at the far end of the pool, head down, and didn't try the dive even once. In the changing room he whispered to Jatin, "Everyone saw me fall. They'll call me Slippy for the whole year."
Jatin was fighting with his goggle strap. "You fell? When?"
"At the start! It was so loud!"
"I was looking for my other flip-flop," Jatin said. "Coach was shouting at Ishani about her cap."
Amandeep stood there with one sock on, thinking. Nobody else in the changing room was talking about it at all.

qa.q: What was Jatin doing in the changing room?
qa.a: Jatin was fighting with the goggle strap.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep stay at the far end of the pool for the rest of the lesson?
qa.a: He felt so embarrassed that he believed the whole class had seen him fall and would call him Slippy all year, so he tried to hide.

qa.q: What small step could Amandeep take at the next class?
qa.a: He could try the dive, remembering that Jatin didn't even see him fall and nobody in the changing room was talking about it.

qa.q: How did Jatin's afternoon look different from how Amandeep imagined it?
qa.a: Jatin was busy looking for a lost flip-flop and struggling with the goggle strap, so the fall went completely unseen.

grounding: It shows a boy who slipped at the pool believing everyone saw and would remember, while others were busy with their own concerns.
